content.title: THE GROCERY STORE SWAPS THAT QUIETLY {{OUTPERFORM}} THE 'HEALTHY' CHOICE
facts: A cup of cooked **swiss chard** has nearly double the magnesium of a cup of spinach, and most people never put it in the cart.
**Brazil nuts** are so loaded with selenium that just 2 nuts/day covers your entire daily need — more than any other common food.
**Dried apricots** carry more iron per cup than a 6oz serving of ground beef, which surprises most people who think iron means meat.
A medium **parsnip** has more fiber than a cup of oatmeal, yet it almost never shows up on 'high-fiber food' lists.
**Dried figs** (5 pieces/day) pack more calcium than a glass of milk, making them a sneaky win for people who skip dairy.
**White beans** (1 cup) have more potassium than a banana — almost double, in fact — but bananas still get all the credit.
**Canned sardines** with bones are one of the few whole foods naturally rich in vitamin D, rivaling a glass of fortified milk per serving.
**Hemp seeds** (3 tbsp/day) deliver a solid dose of plant-based omega-3s, something most people assume only comes from fish.
**Dark leafy kale** carries more vitamin K in a single cup than most people get from an entire day of regular meals.
**Follow along** – for more daily health tips like this.
content.caption:
A few of these deserve a closer look. **Brazil nuts** work so well for selenium because your thyroid actually needs this mineral to convert thyroid hormone into its active form — without enough of it, your metabolism can quietly slow down. **Swiss chard** pulls ahead on magnesium partly because it's so nutrient-dense per calorie, and magnesium is the mineral your muscles and nervous system rely on to actually relax after they contract — low levels are linked to that wired-but-tired feeling. And **sardines** are one of the rare whole-food sources of vitamin D because, unlike most fish, you eat the skin and small bones, where a lot of that fat-soluble vitamin gets stored. Everyone's body and needs are different, so treat this as a starting point, not a prescription.
